posts.title: What a procurement workshop taught me about where AI should stop
posts.summary: Three days in Batam with the people who buy for Pupuk Indonesia Group. What I learned about procurement, how we matched their ideas to PINTER, and why the most useful thing AI can do there is hand over references, not decisions.

toc.label: How procurement works, from the user's side
A problem that was not on the list

posts.html:
From 20 to 22 October 2026, Pupuk Indonesia Group held a focus group discussion in Batam on agentic and generative AI for procurement. I went with my team: Dommy Asfiandy, our VP, Windiarta, an AI engineer, and Laugiwa, a forward deployed engineer.

Most days I write code. That week I sat at the same table as the people who would use it.

Why we were there

PINTER is the internal AI agent platform we build at Pupuk Indonesia. Teams use it to build agents that search documents, call tools, and run multi-step workflows.

Procurement already has its own system for requests, tenders, and contracts. The question for us was simple: which of the users' ideas could run as agents on PINTER, and which belong in the procurement system itself?

We introduced PINTER to the room, then spent most of the time listening.

How procurement works, from the user's side

Before this, I knew procurement as a set of screens. In the room, I saw it as a long chain of people and documents.

A user raises a request for a material or a service. Someone writes the specification. Someone estimates the price. Someone drafts the tender documents. Then come vendors, bids, negotiation, the contract, delivery, and the invoice. Each step has its own owner and its own rules.

What surprised me was how much of the work is searching. What did we pay last time? Is this item the same as one we already stock under another name? Which vendor can supply it? Which regulation applies? People spend hours finding things before they can decide anything.

Sorting the ideas

Participants worked in four breakout rooms and wrote a long list of ideas. Our job was to map them.

The first cut was the most useful one: is this really an AI problem? Many ideas were not. A missing notification, a clearer form, a better report. Those are digitisation work, and they belong in the procurement system. Calling them AI would only make them slower to ship.

The AI ideas fell into a few families: contracts and tender documents, sourcing and vendors, bid evaluation and negotiation, pricing and specifications, receiving and invoices, and a helpdesk that answers questions.

Most of the parts already exist in PINTER: multi-agent workflows, search over a knowledge base, document parsing, scheduled agents, chat channels, structured output, and guardrails. The main missing piece is connectors to the systems where the live data sits.

We also looked for quick wins. The rule we were given scored no AI idea as a quick win. So we used a different filter: it runs on uploaded documents with no integration, it uses parts PINTER already has, and many people asked for it. A helpdesk that answers vendor questions from the SOPs and FAQs, day and night, came out on top.

Breakout room 4: the users

I spent most of my time in the user room. These are the people who raise requests, not the procurement team.

Their problems came down to three things:

  • Finding references. Prices, specifications, and vendors.
  • Writing documents. Tender documents and price estimates.
  • Knowing where a request is. Who has it now, and why it is stuck.

Before we talked about fixes, I explained how PINTER works under the hood: how agents search documents, call tools, and hand work to each other. It helped people see what an assistant could and could not do.

Many of their ideas pointed to the same place: the request form. So instead of many separate agents, they need one assistant that sits next to the form while they fill it in. It can find equivalent materials, draft tender documents, and suggest prices and vendors.

Finding equivalent materials was my favourite. The same item is often written in different ways. Search by meaning, not by exact words, finds them. It also helps one subsidiary borrow stock from another.

Price references can start from uploaded price data and move to live data later. Vendor references wait on live data from the procurement system.

Where AI should stop

This was the most important part of the discussion for me.

Some answers have legal or financial weight. For those, a model should never be the source:

  • The price estimate formula stays in the procurement system. The user and the pricing team must get the same number, so it has to be a fixed formula. AI can only suggest reference prices.
  • Vendor status comes from the system of record. Whether a vendor is blacklisted or suspended is a fact, not a guess.
  • Local content percentage uses a fixed formula. AI helps find the references, nothing more.

I liked this because it is also good engineering. A fact that someone could be audited on should come from a database, not from text a model generated.

A problem that was not on the list

Not every useful problem was on the agenda. While we talked through requests in breakout room 4, people kept bringing up a topic that none of the workshop themes covered.

That topic was contract management: a database of contracts and purchase orders, digital contracts, and clause review.

That sounded familiar. I had built something close for logistics: a tool that keeps carrier contracts and tariffs in one database instead of spreadsheets, with a preview before any import overwrites data. The same approach fits procurement contracts. Keep them in one place, check imports before they land, and let an agent help review the clauses.

I shared that, and suggested the group decide who owns contract management before two teams build it twice.

What I took home

  • Not every problem is an AI problem. Sorting AI from plain digitisation first saved the most time.
  • Users want fewer tools, not more agents. One assistant in the right place beats many clever ones.
  • Draw the boundary early. Deciding what AI must not do made the rest of the design easy.
  • Listen past the agenda. A problem one team raises is often one another team already solved.
  • Engineers should be in these rooms. I learned more about procurement in three days than from any spec.

Next

We are writing up the results with the other teams and helping set priorities. The first agents will be the ones that work on uploaded documents, so users can try them before any integration is ready.

Thanks to Pak Dommy, Windiarta, and Laugiwa, and to everyone in breakout room 4 for their patience with my questions.

posts.title: A triage step for AI models, built on Jev
posts.summary: How I used TypeSafe's new System One model, Jev, to pick the right model for every message in PINTER, the trade-offs I chose, and what I would change next.

toc.label: Why not ask an LLM to pick
What a System One model is

posts.html:
TypeSafe AI released Jev on 15 September 2026. It is their first "System One" model, and it does not write text. A week later it was the routing step in PINTER, the AI agent platform I build at Pupuk Indonesia. This post covers why I picked it, how the router works, and where it still falls short.

The problem

In PINTER, each agent was tied to one model. That forced a bad choice. Put a strong model behind everything and simple questions cost as much as hard ones. Put a cheap model behind everything and hard questions get weak answers.

Most messages are simple. A greeting, a lookup, a short rewrite. A few need real reasoning. I wanted each message to go to the model that fits it, decided per message, without the user doing anything.

Why not ask an LLM to pick

The common trick is to prompt a language model: "Here are the models. Reply with the name of the best one." It works in a demo. In production it has three problems.

  • The answer is text. You parse it and hope it matches one of your options.
  • There is no confidence. A guess and a sure answer look the same.
  • You pay for a generation step to get one word back.

A router needs a choice from a fixed list, a number that says how sure it is, and a clean way to fail.

What a System One model is

Jev is built for that shape of problem. You send it a state, which is any text, and a set of typed questions. It answers each question with a structured value, not prose. There are three question types:

Type Asks Returns
Choice Which option fits? choice, probabilities, confidence
Score How does this rate on a rubric? score, probabilities, confidence
Noul Is this statement true? a value from 0 to 1

A Choice question is a router. The options are my routes, and the confidence tells my code whether to trust the answer. Questions in one call run in parallel, so adding more later barely changes the response time. Input costs $0.042 per million tokens, and there are no output tokens to pay for.

How the router works

PINTER already had virtual models: a name that points to real models. combo tries models in order until one works. round_robin spreads load. I added a third type, smart_router.

An admin sets it up with:

  • Routes. Each route has an intent key, a plain description of what belongs there, and the target model.
  • A fallback model for anything the router cannot place.
  • A confidence threshold, 0.65 by default, adjustable from 0.10 to 0.95.

My router, smart-pinter, has four routes. Cheap text goes to a fast model, tool-heavy steps to a low-latency one, images to a vision model, and hard reasoning or code to the strongest model.

When a message comes in:

  1. PII in the message is masked before anything else sees it.
  2. The router sends the latest user message to Jev as one Choice question. The route descriptions are the options.
  3. Jev returns the chosen intent, its confidence, and the probability of every option.
  4. If the confidence meets the threshold, the message goes to that route's model. Otherwise it goes to the fallback.
  5. The agent runs on the chosen model and streams its answer.
  6. The decision streams to the chat as well, so the user sees it.

The request to Jev looks like this. The descriptions are shortened.

{
  "state": "<latest user message, PII masked>",
  "model": "jev-latest",
  "questions": {
    "intent": {
      "type": "choice",
      "instructions": "Determine the optimal handling tier for this request",
      "criteria": {
        "general_low_cost_text": "High-volume, non-critical text tasks",
        "low_latency_tool_calls": "Text-only tasks that need fast responses",
        "multimodal_vision_processing": "Prompts with images, charts, or scans",
        "advanced_reasoning_and_code": "Complex coding and multi-step reasoning"
      }
    }
  }
}

The decision itself is plain code:

choice, confidence, probabilities = await evaluate_choice(prompt, criteria)

if choice and confidence >= threshold:
    route = find_route(routes, choice)  # case-insensitive match on intent key
    if route:
        return route.target_model_id

return fallback_model_id

That split is the point. Jev makes the judgment. My code decides what to do with it, and the threshold is a setting, not a prompt.

Design decisions

It fails open. If Jev times out after 5 seconds, returns an error, or there is nothing to classify, the message goes to the fallback. The client never raises. A broken triage step should never break the chat.

The threshold is a dial. A high threshold sends more traffic to the fallback. A low one trusts Jev more. Admins tune it per router without touching code.

Only the latest message is classified. This keeps the call small and the result predictable. The cost is that a short follow-up like "and the second one?" is judged without its context.

Private data stays masked. Jev receives the message after PII is replaced with tokens.

Keys live in the vault. The Jev API key can come from a registered model, so it is not stored in the router config. When the config is read back, the key is masked.

No nesting. A route must point to a real model, not another virtual one. That keeps every decision one hop deep and easy to explain.

The decision is visible. Each answer carries a Smart Routing card: the intent, confidence against the threshold, and a bar for every option. It is saved with the message, so it shows up in history and shared chats too.

What a fallback looks like

Not every message fits one route. I asked for a map of fertiliser demand across Indonesia plus a chart of sales trends. Jev's best guess scored only 0.14, far below 0.65. My guess is that the request mixes data lookup, tool calls, and visual output, so no single description matched it well.

The fallback model handled it. It listed the datasets, queried them, and drew both visuals.

This is the case the fallback exists for. It gets every message the router is unsure about, so it has to handle any kind of request, including tool calls. The low score is also a signal: requests like this may deserve their own route.

One bug worth sharing

The first version never matched a single route. Jev was answering correctly. The problem was the config encryptor. It encrypted every field whose name contained "key", to protect secrets. intent_key matched that rule, so every route name was stored encrypted and never equal to Jev's answer. The fix was a short list of exempt field names, plus a test that route names stay readable.

A rough cost estimate

I have not measured savings yet, but list prices give a first idea. The assumptions:

  • 3,000 input and 600 output tokens per message.
  • A traffic mix I guessed: 40% cheap text, 20% tool calls, 10% vision, 15% hard reasoning, 15% fallback.
  • Public list prices on 26 September 2026, off-peak for DeepSeek.
Setup, per 10,000 messages Cost Smart router compared
Smart router, Jev included $21.06 -
Everything on Gemini 3.8 Flash $45.00 53% cheaper
Everything on Deepseek V4 Pro $31.68 34% cheaper
Everything on Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite $24.00 12% cheaper
Everything on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash $8.10 2.6x more expensive

Three things stand out.

  • Jev is close to free. It adds $0.17 per 10,000 messages, under 1% of the bill. It only reads the latest message and has no output tokens.
  • The saving depends on the baseline. Against the strongest model, the router saves about a third. Against the cheapest model, it costs more. What it buys there is quality on the hard messages.
  • The fallback is the biggest lever. At these prices Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite costs more per message than Deepseek V4 Pro, because its output tokens cost more. With 15% of traffic landing there, the fallback choice moves the bill more than any route.

The dollar amounts are small at this scale. The ratio is what matters, and it only holds if the guessed mix is close to real traffic.

What is not measured yet

I would rather say this plainly than guess.

  • Latency. I have not benchmarked the extra time the triage step adds.
  • Cost. The estimate above uses a guessed traffic mix. I have not compared real spend before and after routing.
  • Accuracy. Routing has not been scored against a labelled set of real messages.

These are the next things to measure, and they decide whether the thresholds are right.

What I would change next

  • Retry on the fallback in chat. The OpenAI-compatible endpoint already tries the fallback when the chosen model fails. The chat path does not yet. Both should behave the same.
  • Track the fallback rate. A fallback today only writes a warning to the log. A rising fallback rate is the first sign that routes or thresholds need work, so it should be a metric with an alert.
  • Ask more than one question. Jev evaluates questions in parallel, so one call could return a Choice for the topic and a Score for complexity. My code would combine them. Changing priorities would mean changing a number, not rewriting a prompt.
  • Give follow-ups some context. Classifying the last two or three messages together would fix the "and the second one?" case.

Takeaway

Choosing a model is a decision, not a conversation. Once I treated it that way, the router became small: one typed question, one number, and a few lines of code that decide what to trust. Jev is new, but that idea is the part I would keep with any tool.
